newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FEATURE-Brazil's Indian tribes gather for sporting battle.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Brazil's Indian tribes gather for sporting battle.

text.p: The Fulni-O tribe's soccer team looked unstoppable in Brazil's first national Indigenous Peoples Games, celebrating goal after goal with a ritual victory dance in the centre of the field.

"Football comes naturally to us," boasted midfielder Iratan, recalling that a great-grandfather of Garrincha, the legendary, bow-legged star of Brazil's 1958 and 1962 World Cup-winning teams, was a Fulni-O Indian. But scoring, and celebrating, 31 goals in just three matches must have been exhausting -- the tribe lost the final to the muscular and fiercely competitive Xavantes.

In all, 34 tribes trekked from all over Brazil by boat, bus and plane to the central city of Goiania in October for the five days of the games, bringing with them their body-painted wrestlers and tug-of-war teams, champion archers and tiny women volleyball players.

Many of the 400 participants were making their first trip to a city and walked gingerly in bare feet on the hard pavement. Some grumbled in strange languages about eating food they had not caught or grown themselves. An archer said the noise of traffic disturbed his concentration. And an old man, his lower lip stretched spectacularly around a wooden disc, posed patiently for photographs alongside giggling women.
For almost all the competitors, it was the first time they had shown off their lifestyle to "the whites."

"Despite hundreds of years of contact (with outside society), our culture is still alive. This is a great opportunity to show people what we have," said Kyriwana of the Carajas tribe, due to graduate as a law student this month.

Running, swimming and accuracy with a bow and arrow are skills acquired naturally in day-to-day village life, although it took several explanations by games officials for all of the swimmers to grasp the concept of a race. To most Indians, sport is more about ritual than competition.

Festivals celebrating the souls of the dead traditionally feature wrestlers who accept defeat without the need for a judge. Holy days in some regions begin with crowds of villagers taking turns to shoulder 175-pound (80-kg) tree trunks and run with them through the countryside at dawn.

Where Indians have lost land to farmers and loggers, however, little remains of traditional life. The 900 tribes estimated to have existed in Brazil at the start of the century have dwindled to about 200 now. A third of Brazil's 320,000 Indians are reported to suffer from malnutrition and in some groups -- typically where conflict over land is most fierce -- alcoholism, prostitution and even suicides of children are common.

Some of the most depressed tribes were invited to the games to compete alongside more successful groups in an attempt to instill a sense of Indian identity and pride. The organisers' tactics seemed to have paid off with the swimming victories of the Bororo tribe, one of the worst hit by alcohol and despair. "We wanted to show what Indians are capable of, our beauty and our strength," said games organiser Marcos, a leader of the Terena tribe, as beaming Bororos waved from the top of their medal-winners' podium to cheering spectators.

Photographs of Indian warriors appeared for days in the newspapers of faraway Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro. Ronaldo, Brazil's new soccer idol, dedicated three goals he scored in a match against Lithuania to the Indian athletes, and the archery event was so popular competitors were forced to fire their arrows through a not-so-wide corridor of spectators.
Even two fugitives on the run from a Goiania jail could not stay away from the games and were promptly re-arrested.

"Most people are scared of Indians, they think they're killers," said Antonio Inacio Saza, a security official, as the crowd ignored a rainstorm and cheered on a couple of wrestlers grappling in a circular sandpit.

The spectators suddenly fell silent as four boys were prepared for ritual ear-piercing. Games organiser Marcos explained to the hushed crowd that his Terena tribe had forgotten the rite, which marks the passage to manhood, but that men from the vast Xingu reservation, where the old customs still survive, were ready to teach them.

"We are relearning our tradition," Marcos said through a microphone as the men sang in high-pitched voices and four elders tugged lengths of yellow thread through the boys' ears. Sworn to silence as part of the rite, the youngsters shook their heads convincingly when asked if the needles had hurt.
"Change will always come to our villages but our tradition cannot be allowed to vanish," Marcos said later. "Our tradition is our code, it gives us our identity. Without it we are nothing."
